lessons.title: Open Market Operations and Liquidity: How the RBI Adds and Drains Money

body.text: The repo rate announces the price of money, but liquidity decides whether that price is real. When banks are flooded with cash, overnight rates sink below the repo rate; when cash is scarce, they climb above it. Open market operations are how the RBI adds or removes money that stays in the system for months and years, not just overnight.

children.text: You have seen how the corridor steers overnight rates and how CRR locks away a slice of deposits. This lesson covers the tools the RBI uses to manage the total amount of money in the banking system, and the three dramatic liquidity swings India went through between January 2025 and September 2026.
What "Liquidity" Actually Means

markDefs.definition: The net amount of spare cash banks hold beyond their reserve requirements. In India it is commonly tracked by the net position of banks with the RBI in the liquidity adjustment facility: net parking with the RBI means surplus, net borrowing means deficit.

children.text: When market reports say liquidity is in surplus or deficit, they mean
banking system liquidity

: the spare cash banks have beyond what they must hold. If banks are parking more money with the RBI than they are borrowing from it, the system is in surplus. If they are net borrowers, it is in deficit.

columns.label: Surplus liquidity
points: Banks have more cash than they can lend
Call rate drifts towards the SDF floor, below the repo rate
Money market and short-term bond yields fall
Policy is effectively looser than the repo rate suggests
RBI may drain cash through VRRR auctions or OMO sales

columns.label: Deficit liquidity
points: Banks are short of cash and compete to borrow
Call rate climbs towards the MSF ceiling, above the repo rate
Deposit and short-term borrowing rates rise
Policy is effectively tighter than the repo rate suggests
RBI may inject cash through VRR auctions, swaps or OMO purchases

markDefs.definition: The longer-lasting surplus or deficit in the banking system after stripping out temporary effects, such as government cash balances. It is what OMOs and long-term swaps are used to manage.

children.text: Analysts also separate short-lived swings from
durable liquidity
. A tax payment date might drain cash for a week; a year of heavy currency intervention changes liquidity for months. The RBI uses different tools for each.
The Forces the RBI Does Not Control
Liquidity changes every day for reasons that have nothing to do with monetary policy. The RBI watches these drivers and offsets them.

body.caption: What Adds and Drains Bank Liquidity

cells: People withdraw cash, for example before Diwali or elections
Cash returns to banks after the festive season
Taxes flow in, such as advance tax in mid-March, June, September and December, and GST dates
The government spends on salaries, subsidies and projects
RBI sells dollars to defend the rupee: banks pay rupees, which leave the system
RBI buys dollars from banks: it pays rupees into the system
CRR is raised, or deposits grow and more CRR must be held

body.title: How Much Does a Rupee Defence Drain?
body.prompt: The RBI sells $10 billion in the forex market to stop the rupee from falling. Assume an exchange rate of ₹90 per dollar. How much rupee liquidity does this drain from the banking system, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Banks buying those dollars pay the RBI in rupees: $10,000,000,000 × ₹90 = ₹900,000,000,000. Divide by 1,00,00,000 to convert to crore: ₹90,000 crore. That money leaves banks' accounts and sits with the RBI. This is why heavy currency defence almost always creates a liquidity crunch that the RBI must then fix.

children.text: Open Market Operations: Buying and Selling Bonds

markDefs.definition: The RBI buying or selling government securities in the market. Purchases pay cash into the banking system; sales take cash out. The effect lasts until the bonds mature or the RBI reverses the trade.

children.text: An
open market operation (OMO)
is simply the RBI buying or selling government securities. The logic is mechanical:
OMO purchase:
the RBI buys bonds from banks and pays them rupees. Bank cash goes up. Liquidity is injected.
OMO sale:
the RBI sells bonds to banks and receives rupees. Bank cash goes down. Liquidity is absorbed.

body.title: Direction Check
body.textWithBlank: When the RBI buys government securities through an OMO, it ___ liquidity into the banking system.
body.explanation: It injects liquidity. The RBI pays for the bonds by crediting rupees to banks' accounts, so banks end up with more cash. An OMO sale does the opposite.

children.text: There is a second effect that matters for investors. When the RBI buys bonds, it adds demand, which pushes bond prices up and yields down. When it sells, it adds supply, pushing prices down and yields up. So OMOs move both liquidity and interest rates across the bond market, which you will study closely in Chapter 3.
The RBI announces an OMO auction with the amount and the specific securities it will buy or sell.
Banks, primary dealers and other eligible players submit bids on the RBI's electronic platform.
The RBI accepts bids at prices it considers acceptable, up to the notified amount.
Settlement happens the next working day: cash and bonds change hands, and system liquidity shifts.
The Full Liquidity Toolkit, by How Long the Effect Lasts

body.caption: Matching the Tool to the Problem

cells: Last-resort daily parking and borrowing inside the corridor
Smoothing temporary swings like tax dates
Bridging a tight patch that is expected to pass
Injecting rupee liquidity while also adding to forex reserves
Fixing a long-lasting surplus or deficit
Large system-wide adjustments to lendable cash

markDefs.definition: A deal where a bank sells dollars to the RBI for rupees today and agrees to buy the dollars back at a set date and premium. It injects rupee liquidity for the swap tenor and temporarily adds to forex reserves.

children.text: The
buy/sell swap

deserves a note. A bank sells dollars to the RBI and receives rupees now, then buys the dollars back at a fixed future date. For the life of the swap, banks have more rupees and the RBI has more dollars. It became one of the RBI's favourite tools in 2025.
Case 1: The Crunch of Early 2025

Between late 2024 and early 2025, the RBI sold large amounts of dollars to slow the rupee's fall. Every dollar sold drained rupees. Add advance tax outflows and festive cash withdrawals, and the banking system swung from surplus into its deepest deficit in about 15 years.

body.title: How the RBI Refilled the System

events.title: Deficit peaks near ₹3.15 lakh crore
events.description: The worst shortage of bank cash in roughly 15 years, driven mainly by forex intervention and tax outflows. The call rate rose above the repo rate.

events.title: First package
events.description: OMO purchases of ₹60,000 crore in three tranches, a $5 billion six-month buy/sell swap on 31 January, and a ₹50,000 crore 56-day VRR auction on 7 February to carry banks through the financial year end.

events.title: $10 billion, 3-year swap
events.description: A three-year buy/sell swap injected durable rupee liquidity. The auction was heavily oversubscribed.

events.title: More OMOs and a second big swap
events.description: OMO purchases of ₹1 lakh crore in two tranches on 12 and 18 March, plus another $10 billion three-year swap on 24 March.

events.title: CRR cut announced
events.description: The 100 basis point CRR cut, delivered from September, added about ₹2.5 lakh crore of permanent lendable cash.

body.text: Notice how the RBI layered tools. Quick VRR auctions fixed the immediate squeeze, swaps and OMOs rebuilt durable liquidity, and the CRR cut made it permanent. Each tool matched how long the problem was expected to last.

children.text: Case 2: A Record Year of Bond Buying, FY26

Through 2025-26, the RBI kept buying government bonds to keep liquidity comfortable and help rate cuts reach borrowers. In December 2025 alone, it announced about ₹3 lakh crore of injections: ₹1 lakh crore of OMO purchases on 11 and 18 December, ₹2 lakh crore more in four tranches between 29 December and 22 January 2026, plus buy/sell swaps of $5 billion on 16 December and $10 billion on 13 January 2026. The stated aim was to offset the drain from its rupee defence and seasonal outflows.

stats.label: Share bought by the RBI
stats.context: Nearly half of new central government bonds

body.title: How Much of the Borrowing Did the RBI Absorb?
body.prompt: Between 4 April 2025 and 13 February 2026, the central government borrowed ₹13,65,000 crore through bonds, and the RBI bought ₹6,39,203 crore of government securities through OMOs. What share of the borrowing does that equal, in percent? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹6,39,203 crore ÷ ₹13,65,000 crore × 100 = 46.8%. Close to half. OMO purchases are not direct government funding, since the RBI buys in the secondary market to manage liquidity, but buying on this scale kept bond yields lower than they would otherwise have been.

children.text: Case 3: The Swing to Surplus, 2026

By mid-2026 the problem had flipped. The West Asia conflict pushed oil prices up and the rupee down, so the RBI opened a special swap window in June 2026. Banks that raised fresh FCNR(B) deposits, foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians, could swap those dollars with the RBI for rupees on attractive terms.

body.title: From Dollar Shortage to Rupee Flood

events.title: Special swap window opens
events.description: Covers fresh three to five-year FCNR(B) deposits and certain foreign borrowings. Banks sell the dollars to the RBI and receive rupees, with the trade reversed at maturity.

events.title: Inflows far exceed expectations
events.description: Initial hopes of $50 billion to $60 billion are blown past. The RBI brings the deadline forward from 30 September to 31 August.

events.title: Window closes
events.description: About $136 billion comes in under the facility, including about $127 billion through FCNR(B) deposits.

events.title: Reserves hit a record
events.description: India's forex reserves post their biggest weekly jump ever. But every dollar swapped put rupees into banks, and the call rate sits below the repo rate.

events.title: RBI announces OMO sales
events.description: ₹1 lakh crore of bond sales, maturing between FY29 and FY32, in tranches of ₹50,000 crore on 17 September, ₹25,000 crore on 21 September and ₹25,000 crore on 28 September.

children.text: The market reaction showed OMOs working on both fronts. The 10-year government bond yield rose 6 basis points to about 7.04% and the 5-year yield rose nearly 10 basis points to about 6.62% after the announcement, as traders priced in extra bond supply and less spare cash.

body.title: Why Sell Bonds Instead of Just Running VRRR Auctions?
body.question: In September 2026 the RBI already had reverse repo auctions available to absorb surplus cash. Why did it choose OMO sales?
options: OMO sales are cheaper for the RBI than paying interest on reverse repos
The surplus came from a long-lasting source, so a durable tool was needed rather than repeated short-term operations
VRRR auctions are only allowed during liquidity deficits
OMO sales are the only way to lower bond yields
body.explanation: The FCNR(B) swaps last three to five years, so the rupee liquidity they created is durable. VRRR auctions absorb cash for a few days and must be rolled again and again. An OMO sale removes cash for the life of the bonds sold. The yield effect runs the other way: OMO sales push yields up, not down.

body.title: What Happens to Your Debt Fund?
body.scenario: You hold units of a gilt mutual fund that invests mainly in 5 to 10-year government bonds. On 11 September 2026, the RBI announces ₹1 lakh crore of OMO sales. Your friend panics and wants to redeem immediately.
body.prompt: Explain what the announcement does to your fund's NAV and whether redeeming makes sense.
body.modelAnswer: The NAV will likely dip in the short run. OMO sales add bond supply, pushing prices down and yields up, and gilt funds holding 5 to 10-year bonds are sensitive to that. The 10-year yield rose about 6 basis points and the 5-year about 10 basis points on the announcement, which translates into a small mark-to-market loss. But ask what the RBI is doing and why. It is draining an unusually large surplus, not raising the repo rate, and the size is modest compared with the liquidity created by the swap window. Redeeming locks in the dip and may trigger exit loads or capital gains tax. The better question is whether your holding period and risk tolerance still match a long-duration gilt fund, especially if inflation is heading towards the RBI's projected 5.9% and rate hikes become possible. That is a reason to review your allocation, not a reason to panic-sell on one announcement.

body.title: Go Deeper: Operation Twist and G-SAP, When OMOs Get Creative

children.text: OMOs are not only about adding or draining cash. The RBI has also used them to reshape the yield curve.
Operation Twist, December 2019

Long-term bond yields were staying high even after rate cuts, so the RBI bought ₹10,000 crore of the 6.45% government bond maturing in 2029 while simultaneously selling shorter-dated bonds. Liquidity barely changed, but long-term yields fell sharply, with the 2029 bond's yield dropping by as much as 16 basis points after the operation was announced. The name comes from a similar US Federal Reserve operation in 2011.
G-SAP, 2021

During the pandemic, the RBI launched the Government Securities Acquisition Programme, pre-committing to buy bonds on a set schedule: ₹1 lakh crore in April to June 2021 and ₹1.2 lakh crore in July to September 2021. The pre-announcement itself calmed the bond market by telling investors a big buyer would be there.

cards.definition: Banks' spare cash beyond reserve requirements, tracked by their net position with the RBI.
The longer-lasting surplus or deficit after stripping out temporary swings.
RBI buys government bonds and pays banks rupees: injects liquidity and pushes yields down.
RBI sells government bonds and takes rupees from banks: absorbs liquidity and pushes yields up.
Banks sell dollars to the RBI for rupees now and buy them back later: injects rupees for the swap tenor.
Variable rate repo and reverse repo auctions, used to add or absorb short-term liquidity, mainly for 7 days.
Buying long-term bonds while selling short-term bonds to lower long-term yields without changing total liquidity.

body.label: RBI Homepage: Press Releases
body.description: The RBI publishes a Money Market Operations press release every working day, showing liquidity absorbed and injected, plus separate releases announcing OMO and swap auctions.

body.title: Track Liquidity Like a Bond Trader
steps: Open the RBI's latest Money Market Operations press release and find the net liquidity position
Check whether the call rate is above or below the 5.25% repo rate, and what that says about surplus or deficit
Look up the results of the September 2026 OMO sale tranches: how much was actually sold?
Note the 10-year government bond yield before and after each tranche
Mark the next advance tax date and GST dates in your calendar and watch what happens to the call rate

points: Liquidity is the spare cash in the banking system; surplus pushes overnight rates below the repo rate and deficit pushes them above it.
Currency demand, government cash balances and RBI forex operations constantly add and drain liquidity outside monetary policy.
OMO purchases inject durable liquidity and lower bond yields; OMO sales absorb it and raise yields.
The RBI matches tools to duration: VRR and VRRR for days, swaps for months or years, OMOs and CRR for durable shifts.
In early 2025 the RBI fixed a deficit near ₹3.15 lakh crore with OMOs, dollar swaps and a CRR cut; in FY26 it bought a record ₹6.39 lakh crore of bonds.
In September 2026, after the FCNR(B) swap window flooded banks with rupees, the RBI turned to ₹1 lakh crore of OMO sales.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment advice. The ₹90 per dollar exchange rate in the exercise is illustrative. Liquidity figures and auction details are as reported up to mid-September 2026 and may be revised.
